- If sentiment shows strong bullish (e.g., 1.00 or 0.50) in recent days, model tends to over-forecast; reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- If sentiment shows strong bearish (e.g., -1.00 or 0.00) in recent days, model tends to under-forecast; increase downward bias or adjust for mean reversion.
- After a sharp spike in price (e.g., >10% from prior peak), model often overshoots and fails to correct — cap forecast at 1–2% above peak or add lagged correction term.
- When sentiment is neutral or mixed (e.g., 0.00 or 0.25), model often drifts toward mean reversion — apply smoothing or decay factor to forecast.
- If true outcome shows strong divergence from forecast in early days (e.g., first 5–7 days), model often fails to capture sudden reversals — adjust for sentiment-driven volatility in first 3–5 days.
- Forecast horizon 30d often overestimates upward trend when sentiment is bullish — reduce forecast slope or apply sentiment-weighted decay.
- If sentiment history includes alternating bullish/bearish signals, model tends to overfit to recent sentiment — use sentiment smoothing or weighted average over 3–5 days.
